findings.text: The opening paragraph says what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. A newcomer can say what this is and why it matters after one paragraph.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page explains why a page on Athena's site is about a different project, firstmate. Without this paragraph, the title would confuse a newcomer.
findings.source: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project ... Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: The title and almost all of the body are about firstmate, not Athena. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to read the small grey intro text to see why. The page never shows the parts of Athena the intro promises, such as the cost of each step, the two models or the verdict.
findings.source: Title / h1: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The next steps are concrete and in order: prerequisites, clone, install, then a first command to try. The link near the top ("Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself") lets a newcomer skip the long study.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm ... Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh ... athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: This line is written for the site's owner, but it sits in the header that every newcomer reads. It is unclear whose decision is meant and whether the visitor should click it.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The Transitions and Counters sections are dense and use ids such as t1 to t12 and c1 to c45. They suit someone checking firstmate's behaviour, not a newcomer deciding whether to try Athena. The "Words used first" list and the Glossary help, but the same terms (yolo, green, in scope) are defined up to three times.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: The links from each claim to exact file lines at a fixed commit show Athena's traceability promise in practice. This is the page's strongest evidence that the tool does what the intro says.
findings.source: "Next steps": "Check a statement: follow a bracketed claim id to the claim, then its source link to the file and lines in firstmate at the pinned commit."

findings.text: This section and the footer mention an internal folder without saying which repository it is in. To a newcomer this is noise.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
